title: eSports Management
desc: Plan and run a small eSports team, club or tournament: roster, schedule, wellbeing, fair play, finance and sponsors.
outcomes: Explain how eSports teams and events work.
Judge wellbeing, fair play and contracts.
task: Plan and run a one-day small tournament or a one-month team season, with roster, rules, wellbeing plan, budget and report.
condition: A game with free play, a computer or consoles, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Rules are published; fair-play and anti-cheat steps are used; wellbeing plan limits hours and includes breaks; budget totals correct; report with results; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Club leaders, coaches, event organisers, students.
evidence: roster, rules, schedule, wellbeing plan, budget, report
modules: The eSports ecosystem and who decides what
Understand
eSports is organised competition in video games. To manage a team or event you must know who owns the game, who runs competitions and who protects players.
The game publisher owns the game and sets licence rules for events, prize pools and streaming.
Leagues and organisers run seasons and tournaments; teams sign and develop players; platforms stream.
Roles around a team: players, coach, analyst, manager, content creator, shoutcaster (match commentator) and referee.
Schools and clubs have their own safeguarding rules, especially for minors.
A school club wants to charge an entry fee. It reads the publisher's community event rules, finds that paid events may need approval, and applies before announcing.
Map the roles and rules for a small club in one chart, with the publisher rules you checked.
Chart lists at least six roles and two rule sources with dates.
Building the roster and the team culture
Apply
A good roster fits skill, communication and schedule. A good culture keeps players improving and staying.
Run trials: scrims (practice matches), a team chat and a review. Watch communication as much as score.
Write expectations: practice days, attendance, language, equipment care and how conflict is handled.
Use written agreements; for under-18s involve parents or guardians.
Equal chance: no discrimination in trials; publish the criteria.
A trial reveals a skilled player who cannot practise after 9 pm. The team moves practice to 7 pm and wins the player's commitment.
Build a roster of five plus two substitutes with roles and write a one-page team agreement.
Cover all roles in the roster; cover schedule, conduct and conflict handling in the agreement.
Practice, review and improvement
Analyse
Teams improve by reviewing real play, not by playing more hours.
Record matches and tag errors by type such as positioning, timing, communication and decision.
Choose one focus per week and drill it in short blocks.
Use stats such as objectives taken, deaths per round and win rate by map.
Give feedback in a fixed pattern: one positive, one fix, one drill.
Review shows the team loses objectives at the 10-minute mark. Two drills and a call sheet cut lost objectives from 6 to 3 per match in four weeks.
Review one recorded match and write three findings, three drills and one measure.
Base the findings on the data and give each drill a measure.
Wellbeing, study and safety
Evaluate
Long hours at screens harm health and results.
Sleep seven to nine hours; eat regularly; drink water.
Stretch wrists, shoulders and neck; rest eyes every 20 minutes.
Cap practice hours and protect study or work time.
Know signs of burnout and where to get help.
A coach limits practice to three hours a day, adds a rest day and a wrist stretch routine. Reports of wrist pain fall to zero in six weeks.
Write a 7-day schedule that includes practice, study, sleep, exercise and rest.
Schedule shows sleep of at least seven hours and a weekly rest day.
Fair play, conduct and integrity
Evaluate
Cheating and abuse destroy trust.
Ban cheat software, account sharing and match fixing.
Use a ladder of sanctions: warning, short ban, season ban, permanent ban.
Provide an appeals route and a reporting channel.
Protect minors: no private messages with adults; keep contact in group channels.
A player is banned for a season after cheat software is found by the platform. The team publishes the ruling and the appeal result.
Draft a code of conduct and a sanctions ladder.
Write a code with at least six rules and a four-step ladder.
Running a tournament
Create
A good tournament is mostly planning.
Choose format: single or double elimination, round robin or groups.
Plan matches per station; add time for tech delays; assign referees.
Publish rules, schedule and prize details before registration.
Keep spare devices, cables and a technical helper.
A 16-team double-elimination bracket needs about 30 matches. With 40 minutes per match and two stations it takes about 10 hours, so a third station is added to finish in 7.
Build a bracket, schedule and referee plan for 8 teams.
Schedule has no clashes and a delay allowance of 15 per cent.
Budget, sponsors and honesty
Analyse
Money must be clear to players, teams and sponsors.
List costs: venue, equipment, internet, staff, prizes, insurance, marketing.
List income: entry fees, sponsors, tickets and merchandise.
Disclose sponsors and prize rules to everyone.
Keep receipts and a simple ledger.

Twelve teams at an entry fee of 2,000 INR per team (an estimate; check your market) give 24,000 INR; costs are 22,000 INR, so break-even is 11 teams (22,000 / 2,000) and the surplus is 2,000 INR; a sponsor adds 15,000 INR for prizes.
Build a one-page budget with a break-even number of teams.
Calculate totals correctly and show break-even.
Report, review and next season
Create
Learn from each event.
Compare plan and actual for time, cost and attendance.
Survey players and spectators with five questions.
List three improvements and owners.
Share a short report with thanks.
Feedback shows long waits between matches; the next event adds a third station and a clearer schedule board.
Write a one-page event report.
Report has numbers, feedback and three dated improvements.
rubric: Match results and any disputes logged
Disputes traced to rules and one rule changed
Age limit, prize rules and break rules for the place are written down
Rules checked and a wellbeing check practised
local: Age rules, gambling-related rules and contracts differ by place.
